title: Apple Dictation alternatives for Mac in 2026: price, privacy and what each app does best
metaTitle: Apple Dictation Alternatives for Mac in 2026 Compared
description: Apple Dictation alternatives for Mac compared on price, privacy, platforms and features. See where Apple Dictation and Siri win, and where Lazur fits.
intro: Apple Dictation alternatives for Mac split into two groups. Some tools only type what you say, and others also answer questions and take actions. This page compares Apple Dictation, Siri and Lazur on price, platforms, privacy and the features that matter in daily work. Apple's pages list no price for Dictation or Siri, so the table says so instead of guessing.
tldr: Apple Dictation is built into macOS. It stops after 30 seconds without speech, and its on-device English model needs M3 or later with 12GB of memory.
Siri AI is an English-only beta on the pages checked. Apple's pages list no price for Siri or Dictation.
Lazur adds a voice assistant that points at things on screen, plus dictation with snippets and a personal dictionary. It starts with a 3-day Pro trial.
Pick Apple Dictation for a built-in tool. Pick Lazur for help with what is on screen. Pick Siri if you want Apple's assistant and can wait for it to mature.

blocks.text: What Apple Dictation does well on a Mac

Apple Dictation ships with macOS, so there is no separate app to install. You turn it on in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation. Apple's Mac help guide says you can dictate text of any length without a timeout. For long drafts, that matters more than any extra feature.

It also runs on the device for English, but only on the right hardware. Apple says the on-device model for spelling, punctuation and capitalization is available in English on Mac models with M3 and later and at least 12GB of unified memory. Open Apple menu > About This Mac to see your chip and memory before you plan around it. If your Mac falls short, do not assume the on-device model applies to you.

Apple's guide does not state a price for Dictation, so you will not find one there. The same is true of Siri, as covered below. That is why the price line in this comparison reads See their pricing page for both Apple products.
Where Apple Dictation runs out of road

The most common snag is silence. Apple's guide says Dictation stops automatically after 30 seconds without detected speech. Say you pause to check a figure in a spreadsheet. If you stay quiet long enough, the session ends. You press the shortcut again and start a new session. The restart costs little time, but it breaks your rhythm.

Dictation types what you say. It does not answer questions about the screen, and it does not take actions for you. Apple's guide also says that when Voice Control is on, standard Dictation is not available. If you rely on Voice Control for clicking, you cannot run both at once.

Some competitor blogs go further. Voibe says Apple Dictation is accurate and responsive for everyday English, and rates it 7/10 without measured accuracy. EmberType says accuracy drifts on passages longer than about 30 seconds, and gives no test method. Both are sales pitches from makers of rival dictation apps, so treat them as opinion and test the claim yourself.
Siri: an assistant, not a like-for-like swap

Siri is Apple's assistant, and the newer Siri AI is the version to watch. Apple's Siri page describes it as a conversational assistant. It answers open-ended questions, uses personal context and takes actions in apps. The same page lists improved Dictation among its features.

Siri AI is still early. Apple's June 2026 newsroom post says developer testing began June 8, 2026, and a public beta is due later this year. The user beta launches in English, with more languages to follow. Mac and Vision Pro users can use it in a supported language. It is not initially available in the EU on iOS, iPadOS or watchOS, and China is excluded while regulatory requirements are worked through.

Reviewers are warm but cautious. MacRumors reviewer Juli Clover called Siri AI the smarter, more capable version of Siri in June 2026. She praised its personal context and cross-app actions. Her main caveat was that Apple is still refining the feature. That is one reviewer's opinion of a beta, not a measure of quality.

For hardware, check Apple's current page before you buy anything. Sources disagree on the iPhone line, so the Mac rules are the safer thing to plan around. Apple's newsroom lists iPad and Mac with M1 or later for Siri AI. The advanced on-device model, used for expressive voices and advanced dictation, needs a Mac with M3 or later and 12GB or more of memory.
Lazur: a voice assistant that sees your screen

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘, which is Option and Command together, to ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud. Ask where something is, and it draws a circle and a label around that thing on your screen.

Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time. It waits for each click. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. You stay in control, and that is a real trade-off. If you want an assistant that acts for you, Lazur is the wrong pick.

For text, hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Lazur also keeps snippets, a personal dictionary and clipboard slots. Dictation is included, and it is unlimited on both paid plans. It is not the headline, but it covers the typing job that Apple Dictation covers.

Everyday tasks work by voice too. Lazur handles timers, Apple Reminders, Calendar events, notes, music and volume, opening apps and links, web search and Shortcuts. Background research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension, then comes back with a summary and a report.
Privacy: what each option says about your audio

Privacy is where the three options differ most in writing. Apple's legal page on Siri and Dictation says your audio is not stored by Apple unless you opt in to Improve Siri and Dictation. With that setting on, Apple will collect, store and review more data, including the audio and text of what you say. You turn it off under Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics & Improvements.

The same Apple page says on-device transcripts stay on the device, and turning off Siri and Dictation deletes them. Apple may retain and use some data for up to two years. Read that line before you dictate client or medical notes. The page does not spell out every data type covered by that window.

Lazur's stated rule is narrower. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those claims come from Lazur's product facts, so check them against the app's current policy before you decide.

Siri's privacy case rests on Private Cloud Compute. Apple's newsroom says that when it handles requests, personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple. Outside experts can verify that promise. Apple does not say what share of requests stays on the device, so do not assume a split.
Price: what you can confirm and what you cannot

Apple's pages do not give a price for Dictation or Siri. The Siri page says expanded access to some server-side features will be available for a fee in the future, and that usage limits may apply. It does not name Dictation in that footnote. Because no price is confirmed, the table says See their pricing page.

Lazur's stated terms are a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. Pro costs $18/month, or $15/month billed annually, with 150 AI actions. Power costs $120/month, or $96/month annually, with 1,000 AI actions. Dictation is unlimited on both plans. Compare the AI action count with how often you ask questions, not how often you type. See [Lazur pricing](/pricing) for the current plan details.
A worked example: a long email you dictate in pieces

Take a long reply to a client. You dictate the greeting and the first paragraph, then pause to find a figure in your spreadsheet. If that pause runs longer than 30 seconds, Apple Dictation stops. You restart the shortcut and carry on. The session works. It just breaks the sentence you were building.

Now try the same email with Lazur. Hold fn and dictate the text, and it lands at the cursor in the app you use. For the figure, hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur what the number is in the spreadsheet on screen. It answers out loud. Lazur's product facts do not list a silence timeout for dictation, so test the pause before you trust it.
Mistakes people make when they switch

items: Assuming Dictation works in your language. Apple says it is not available in all languages or regions, so check your language in the guide first.
Skipping the hardware check. The on-device English model needs M3 or later and at least 12GB of unified memory.
Expecting screen help from Dictation. It types what you say, and Apple's guide describes no screen-aware help.
Planning around Siri AI as if it shipped. The pages checked describe an English-only beta. Check Apple's pages before you plan.
Turning on Voice Control and wondering where Dictation went. Standard Dictation is not available while Voice Control is on.
Treating a competitor's test as your own test. Use your voice, your apps and your pauses.

blocks.text: How to test two options on your Mac in one afternoon

items: Open System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation and confirm it is on. Dictate one paragraph of your real work and count the errors you fix.
Pause mid-sentence for longer than 30 seconds. Note whether the session stops.
Check the Keyboard setting that says whether Dictation is processed on your device, as Apple's guide describes. Write down what your Mac shows.
Download Lazur from the [download page](/download). The 3-day trial starts when you first open the app.
Hold fn and dictate the same paragraph. Count the errors and the pauses, and note how long the fixes take.
Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask a question about something on screen. Check whether Lazur points at it and answers out loud.

blocks.text: Keep the test short, and use real text. An email you have to send today tells you more than any published score. Do not test with a sample sentence, because a sample hides the pauses you actually make.
Which one should you pick

Pick Apple Dictation if you want a built-in tool, you dictate English on a supported Mac, and you rarely pause for long. It costs nothing to try, since it is already on the Mac. Check the on-device line in Keyboard settings first.

Pick Lazur if you want dictation plus a voice assistant that sees your screen, points at things and handles timers, reminders and calendar events. Accept that it guides you through clicks rather than clicking for you.

Pick Siri, or wait for Siri AI, if you already live in Apple's ecosystem and want personal context from your own devices. Accept that the beta is English only for now, and that Apple has not published a price for it.

For the head-to-head with Lazur, read [Lazur vs Apple Dictation on Mac](/compare/lazur-vs-apple-dictation). For a broader look at built-in and third-party dictation, read [Apple dictation vs AI dictation apps](/blog/apple-dictation-vs-ai-dictation).
Start with the hardware check and the language check. Then run the 30 second pause test. Those three steps settle most of the choice before you compare features.

faq.question: Is Apple Dictation free on Mac?
faq.answer: Apple's Mac help guide does not state a price for Dictation, and Apple's Siri page does not either. No price is confirmed, so this comparison says See their pricing page. Dictation is turned on in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation.

faq.question: Does Apple Dictation work offline?
faq.answer: Apple's guide does not state an internet requirement or offline availability for Dictation. It says you can check Keyboard settings to see whether general Dictation is processed on your device and not sent to Siri servers. Check that line on your own Mac before you rely on it offline.

faq.question: How long can you dictate with Apple Dictation?
faq.answer: Apple says you can dictate text of any length without a timeout. Dictation stops automatically after 30 seconds without detected speech. A long pause ends the session, so you press the shortcut again and continue.

faq.question: Is Siri AI available on Mac now?
faq.answer: Apple's pages describe Siri AI as a beta. The pages checked say it is English only, and a public beta is due later this year. Check Apple's current pages for release status on your Mac, because this page did not confirm a shipped version.

faq.question: Does Lazur replace Apple Dictation?
faq.answer: Lazur can dictate with hold fn and types clean text at the cursor in any app. It also answers questions about your screen, which Apple's Mac guide does not describe for Dictation. Test the pause and language on your own Mac first, because Lazur's product facts do not list a silence timeout or a language list.

faq.question: Does Lazur click buttons for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. Ask how to do something, and it guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. It also circles and labels things you ask about on screen.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned but not available.

faq.question: Which option keeps your audio more private?
faq.answer: Each option makes its own claims, and this page did not test any of them. Apple says audio is not stored unless you opt in to Improve Siri and Dictation. Lazur says it listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut. Compare both sets of claims against the policy pages before you decide.

verdict: Keep Apple Dictation if you want a built-in tool for English and you rarely pause for long. Pick Lazur if you want dictation plus a voice assistant that points at things on screen and guides you through clicks. Pick Siri if you live in Apple's ecosystem and can wait for Siri AI to leave beta. Check your chip, memory and language first, because those settle the choice more than any feature list.
